title: IX. The Sensualists
paragraphs: Grigory and Smerdyakov ran into the room right after Dmitri. They'd been struggling with him in the passage, trying to keep him out, following instructions Fyodor Pavlovitch had given them some days before. Taking advantage of the moment Dmitri paused to look around the room after entering, Grigory ran around the table, shut the double doors on the far side leading to the inner rooms, and planted himself in front of them, arms spread wide, ready to defend the entrance, as it were, with the last drop of his blood. Seeing this, Dmitri let out something more like a scream than a shout and lunged at Grigory.
"So she's there! She's hiding in there! Out of my way, you scoundrel!"

He tried to drag Grigory aside, but the old servant shoved him back. Beside himself with fury, Dmitri struck out and hit Grigory with all his strength. The old man dropped like a log, and Dmitri, leaping right over him, broke through the door. Smerdyakov stood pale and trembling at the far end of the room, pressed close against Fyodor Pavlovitch.
"She's here!" Dmitri shouted. "I saw her turn toward the house just now, but I couldn't catch her. Where is she? Where is she?"
That single cry, "She's here!" had an indescribable effect on Fyodor Pavlovitch. Every trace of his terror vanished.

"Hold him! Hold him!" he cried, and dashed after Dmitri. Meanwhile Grigory had gotten up off the floor, but still seemed dazed. Ivan and Alyosha ran after their father. In the third room, something fell to the floor with a ringing crash -- a large glass vase, not an expensive one, on a marble pedestal, which Dmitri had knocked over as he ran past.
"After him!" shouted the old man. "Help!"
Ivan and Alyosha caught the old man and forcibly hauled him back.
"Why are you running after him? He'll murder you outright," Ivan cried furiously at his father.
"Ivan! Alyosha! She has to be here. Grushenka's here. He said he saw her himself, running."
He was choking. He hadn't been expecting Grushenka at all, and the sudden news that she was here had made him beside himself. He was shaking all over. He seemed frantic.
"But you've seen for yourself that she hasn't come," cried Ivan.
"But she might have come in by that other entrance."
"You know that entrance is locked, and you have the key."

Dmitri suddenly reappeared in the drawing room. He had, of course, found the other entrance locked, and the key was indeed in Fyodor Pavlovitch's pocket. The windows of every room were shut too, so Grushenka couldn't have come in anywhere, and couldn't have run out anywhere either.

"Hold him!" shrieked Fyodor Pavlovitch, the moment he saw him again. "He's been stealing money out of my bedroom." And, tearing himself free of Ivan, he rushed at Dmitri again. But Dmitri threw up both hands and suddenly seized the old man by the two tufts of hair left on his temples, yanked at them, and flung him crashing to the floor. He kicked him two or three times in the face with his heel. The old man let out a shrill moan. Ivan, though not as strong as Dmitri, threw his arms around him and pulled him away with all his might. Alyosha helped too, with his slender strength, holding Dmitri back from the front.
"Madman! You've killed him!" cried Ivan.
"Serves him right!" shouted Dmitri, breathless. "If I haven't killed him, I'll come back and finish the job. You can't protect him forever!"
"Dmitri! Leave, right now!" Alyosha cried, commanding.
"Alexey! Tell me. You're the only one I can believe; was she here just now, or not? I saw her myself, creeping this way along the fence from the lane. I shouted, and she ran."
"I swear she hasn't been here, and no one was expecting her."

"But I saw her.... So she must... I'll find out right now where she is.... Goodbye, Alexey! Not a word to Aesop about the money now. But go to Katerina Ivanovna at once, and be sure to tell her: 'He sends his compliments to you!' His compliments, his compliments! Just compliments, and farewell! Describe the whole scene to her."

Meanwhile Ivan and Grigory had lifted the old man and settled him into an armchair. His face was covered in blood, but he was conscious, and listened greedily to Dmitri's shouting. He was still convinced that Grushenka really was somewhere in the house. Dmitri looked at him with hatred as he went out.
"I don't regret spilling your blood!" he cried. "Beware, old man, beware of your dream, because I have a dream of my own too. I curse you, and I disown you completely."
He ran out of the room.
"She's here. She must be here. Smerdyakov! Smerdyakov!" the old man wheezed, barely audible, beckoning with his finger.
"No, she's not here, you old lunatic!" Ivan shouted at him angrily. "Look, he's fainting! Water! A towel! Hurry, Smerdyakov!"

Smerdyakov ran for water. They finally got the old man undressed and put him to bed. They wrapped a wet towel around his head. Worn out from the brandy, the violent emotion, and the blows he'd taken, he closed his eyes and fell asleep the moment his head touched the pillow. Ivan and Alyosha went back to the drawing room. Smerdyakov cleared away the pieces of the broken vase, while Grigory stood by the table, staring gloomily at the floor.
"Shouldn't you put a wet bandage on your own head and go to bed too?" Alyosha said to him. "We'll look after him. My brother gave you a terrible blow -- on the head."
"He's insulted me!" Grigory pronounced, gloomy and distinct.
"He's insulted his father, not just you," Ivan observed, with a forced smile.
"I used to wash him in his own tub. And he's insulted me," Grigory repeated.
"Damn it all, if I hadn't pulled him off, he might have killed him. It wouldn't take much to finish off Aesop, would it?" Ivan whispered to Alyosha.
"God forbid!" cried Alyosha.
"Why should he forbid it?" Ivan went on, still in a whisper, with a malicious twist to his mouth. "One reptile will devour the other. And serve them both right, too."
Alyosha shuddered.
"Of course I won't let him be murdered, any more than I did just now. Stay here, Alyosha, I'm going to take a turn in the yard. My head's started aching."

Alyosha went to his father's bedroom and sat beside the bed, behind the screen, for about an hour. The old man suddenly opened his eyes and stared at Alyosha for a long while, clearly remembering, clearly thinking things over. All at once his face showed extraordinary agitation.
"Alyosha," he whispered anxiously, "where's Ivan?"
"In the yard. He's got a headache. He's keeping watch."
"Give me that hand mirror. It's over there. Give it to me."

Alyosha handed him the little round folding mirror that stood on the chest of drawers. The old man looked at himself in it; his nose was considerably swollen, and on the left side of his forehead there was a large crimson bruise.
"What does Ivan say? Alyosha, my dear, my only son, I'm afraid of Ivan. I'm more afraid of Ivan than of the other one. You're the only one I'm not afraid of...."
"Don't be afraid of Ivan either. He's angry, but he'll defend you."
"Alyosha, and what about the other one? He's run off to Grushenka. My angel, tell me the truth -- was she here just now, or not?"
"No one saw her. It was a mistake. She hasn't been here at all."
"You know Mitya wants to marry her -- marry her."
"She won't marry him."
"She won't. She won't. She won't. She won't, no matter what!"

The old man positively fluttered with joy, as though nothing more comforting could have been said to him. In his delight he seized Alyosha's hand and pressed it warmly to his heart. Tears actually glistened in his eyes.

"That image of the Mother of God I was telling you about just now," he said. "Take it home and keep it for yourself. And I'll let you go back to the monastery.... I was only joking this morning, don't be angry with me. My head hurts, Alyosha.... Alyosha, comfort my heart. Be an angel and tell me the truth!"
"You're still asking whether she's been here or not?" Alyosha asked, sorrowfully.

"No, no, no. I believe you. Here's what I want: you go to Grushenka yourself, or find some way to see her; hurry, ask her; find out for yourself which of us she means to choose, him or me. Eh? What? Can you do that?"
"If I see her, I'll ask her," Alyosha muttered, embarrassed.
"No, she won't tell you," the old man broke in. "She's a rogue. She'll start kissing you and say it's you she wants. She's a deceitful, shameless hussy. You mustn't go near her, you mustn't!"
"No, father, and it wouldn't be suitable anyway, it wouldn't be right at all."
"Where was he sending you just now? He shouted 'Go' as he ran off."
"To Katerina Ivanovna's."
"For money? To ask her for money?"
"No. Not for money."

"He hasn't got a farthing. I'll settle in for the night now, and think things over, and you can go. Maybe you'll run into her.... Only be sure to come to me tomorrow morning. Be sure to. I've got something to tell you tomorrow. Will you come?"
"Yes."
"When you come, pretend you've come of your own accord, just to ask how I am. Don't tell anyone I asked you to. Not a word to Ivan."
"Very well."
"Goodbye, my angel. You stood up for me just now. I'll never forget it. I've got something to tell you tomorrow -- but I have to think it over first."
"And how are you feeling now?"
"I'll get up tomorrow and go out, perfectly well, perfectly well!"

Crossing the yard, Alyosha found Ivan sitting on the bench by the gate. He was sitting there, writing something in pencil in his notebook. Alyosha told Ivan that their father had woken up, was conscious, and had sent him back to sleep at the monastery.
"Alyosha, I'd be very glad to meet you tomorrow morning," said Ivan cordially, standing up. His warmth caught Alyosha completely off guard.
"I'll be at the Hohlakovs' tomorrow," Alyosha answered, "and I may go to Katerina Ivanovna's too, if I don't manage to find her now."
"But you're going to see her now, anyway? For that 'compliments and farewell'?" Ivan said, smiling. Alyosha looked flustered.
"I think I understand his outburst just now, and part of what led up to it, well enough. Dmitri's asked you to go to her and tell her that he -- well, in short -- is taking his leave of her?"
"Brother, how will all this horror end, between father and Dmitri?" Alyosha exclaimed.
"There's no telling for certain. Maybe it'll come to nothing: it might all fizzle out. That woman's a beast. In any case, we have to keep the old man indoors and not let Dmitri into the house."
"Brother, let me ask you one more thing: does any man have the right to look at other men and decide who deserves to live?"
"Why bring worth into it at all? The matter's usually settled in men's hearts on much more ordinary grounds than that. And as for rights -- who doesn't have the right to wish for something?"
"Not for another man's death?"

"What if it were for another man's death? Why lie to ourselves, since everyone lives this way, and perhaps can't help living this way. Are you referring to what I said just now -- that one reptile will devour the other? In that case let me ask you: do you think I'm capable, like Dmitri, of spilling Aesop's blood -- of murdering him, eh?"
"What are you saying, Ivan? A thought like that never crossed my mind. I don't think Dmitri's capable of it either."

"Thanks, if only for that," Ivan smiled. "Rest assured, I'd always defend him. But when it comes to my own wishes, I reserve myself full latitude in this case. Goodbye till tomorrow. Don't condemn me, and don't think of me as a villain," he added, with a smile.
They shook hands warmly, as they'd never done before. Alyosha felt that his brother had taken the first step toward him, and that he'd certainly done it with some particular purpose in mind.
